Egyptian Dynasties. The system of periodization used to organize ancient Egypt's three-millennia history into distinct royal houses and cultural epochs. Scholars divide the span from circa thirty-one hundred BCE with unification under the First Dynasty to thirty BCE with Roman conquest into major kingdoms: the Old Kingdom as the pyramid-building era, the Middle Kingdom as the classical age, and the New Kingdom as the imperial peak—separated by "intermediate periods" of fragmentation. This framework maps the rise and fall of dynasties, shifting power centers, and transformations in art, religion, and statecraft.

The Old Kingdom from circa twenty-six eighty-six to twenty-one eighty-one BCE was the pyramid age. The Great Pyramids of Giza and the Sphinx were built under the Fourth Dynasty, centered in Memphis. It collapsed into fragmentation.

The Middle Kingdom from circa twenty fifty-five to sixteen fifty BCE saw cultural and administrative consolidation. Art and literature flourished. Egypt extended control to Nubia. It ended with invasion by the Hyksos.

The New Kingdom from circa fifteen fifty to ten seventy BCE was Egypt's imperial zenith. Thebes became the capital. Pharaohs like Thutmose the Third and Ramesses the Second commanded vast territories. Temples and tombs, including the Valley of the Kings, reached monumental scale.

The Ptolemaic dynasty from three hundred five to thirty BCE was founded by Alexander the Great's general after his death. Greek-speaking, it ruled from Alexandria and blended Greek and Egyptian culture. Cleopatra the Seventh was its last ruler.

Major breaks—the First and Second Intermediate Periods—marked times when central authority fragmented and regional governors called nomarchs held power. The entire chronology depends on overlapping king lists, astronomical alignments, and textual references. Exact dates remain debated by Egyptologists.

Dynasties were matrilineal in some periods. Succession sometimes followed the female line, and marriage between relatives was practiced. Egyptian Dynasties connects to ancient Egypt as the civilization whose history the dynasty system periodizes, to the pharaoh as the divine rulers who constituted each dynasty's lineage, to the Nile River as the geographic axis that determined where capitals arose and cultural centers shifted, to Cleopatra as the final Ptolemaic ruler whose reign ended with Rome's conquest of Egypt, to the Pyramids as monumental tombs built by Old Kingdom pharaohs especially the Fourth Dynasty, and to hieroglyphics as the writing system that preserved records of dynasties, kings, and events via inscriptions and papyri.
